statement.p: (a) Show that each of the vector fields \vec F = 3y\,\vec i + 3x\,\vec j, \vec G = \frac{2 y}{x^2 + y^2}\,\vec i + \frac{-2 x}{x^2 + y^2}\,\vec j, and \vec H = \frac{5 x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}\,\vec i + \frac{5 y}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}\,\vec j are gradient vector fields on some domain (not necessarily the whole plane) by finding a potential function for each.

(b) Find the line integrals of \vec F,\vec G,\vec H around the curve C given to be the unit circle in the xy-plane, centered at the origin, and traversed counterclockwise.
(c) For which of the three vector fields can Green's Theorem be used to calculate the line integral in part (b)?

It may be used for
?
only F
only G
only H
F and G
F and H
G and H
F, G and H

p.em: (Be sure that you are able to explain why or why not.)

static.solution:
(a) We see that \vec F,\vec G,\vec H are all gradient vector fields, since 
abla (3xy) = \vec F\quad\mbox{for all }x,y, 
abla (2	an^{-1}\mathopen{}\left( rac{x}{y}ight)) = \vec G\quad\mbox{except where }y=0, and 
abla (5\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}) = \vec H\quad\mbox{except at }(0,0). Other answers are possible.
(b) Parameterizing the unit circle, C, by x=\cos t, y=\sin t, 0\le t\le 2\pi, we have \vec r'(t) =-\sin t\,\vec i+ \cos t\,\vec j, so \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = 3\int_0^{2\pi}((\sin t)\vec i+(\cos t)\vec j)\cdot ((-\sin t)\vec i+(\cos t)\vec j)\,dt = 3\int_0^{2\pi}\cos (2t)\,dt = 0. The vector field \vec G is tangent to the circle, pointing in the opposite direction to the parameterization, and of length 2 everywhere. Thus \int_C\vec G\cdot d\vec r= -2\cdot\hbox{ Length of circle }=-4\pi. The vector field \vec H points radially outward, so it is perpendicular to the circle everywhere. Thus \int_C\vec H\cdot d\vec r = 0.
(c) Green's Theorem does not apply to the computation of the line integrals for \vec G and \vec H because their domains do not include the origin, which is in the interior, R, of the circle. Green's Theorem does apply to \vec F=3y\vec i+3x\vec j. \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_R\left( rac{\partial}{\partial x} F_2 -  rac{\partial}{\partial y} F_1ight)\,dx\,dy = \int 0\,dx\,dy=0.
